title: China and Japan: Scholars and Samurai
bigQuestion: What happens when a society's official ranking of people no longer matches who holds wealth and power?

story.title: The Bow on the Bridge
story.kicker: A rich merchant in old Edo steps aside for a poor samurai, because the law says rank matters more than money.
paragraphs: Picture a spring morning in Edo, the city we now call Tokyo, around the year 1750. A cloth merchant we will call Kichibei walks across a wooden bridge. His shop is one of the busiest in the city. Lords borrow money from men like him. He eats well and lives in a large house behind his shop.

Coming the other way is a samurai. His robe is faded and patched. His rice stipend, the yearly pay his lord gives him, has not risen in years, and he owes money to shopkeepers. But two swords hang at his waist. Only samurai were allowed to wear two swords in public.

Kichibei stops, steps to the side of the bridge and bows low. The samurai walks past without a word. Kichibei knows the rules. Under the Tokugawa government, samurai stood at the top of the official order. Merchants stood at the bottom of the four ranks, no matter how rich they were. A merchant who was rude to a samurai could be punished severely.

Yet by evening, the same samurai may visit Kichibei's shop to ask for more time on a debt. This was the puzzle of Tokugawa Japan. The official ranking said one thing. Money often said another. Over time, that gap helped push Japan toward great change.
story.think: Who really had more power on that bridge, the merchant or the samurai? What kinds of power can a person have?

lessons.title: Four Kinds of People
lessons.mainIdea: Chinese thinkers ranked society as scholars, farmers, artisans and merchants.
reading: Confucius was a teacher who lived in China about 2,500 years ago. He taught that society works best when people know their roles and act with respect. Rulers should be wise and caring. Children should honor parents. Later thinkers who followed his ideas are called Confucians.

Confucian writers described four kinds of people. At the top were *scholars*, educated men who served in government. Next came farmers, who grew the food everyone needed. Then artisans, who made tools and goods. Last came merchants, who bought and sold. Many writers called merchants less useful because they did not produce things themselves.

This ranking was an ideal, not a set of castes. People were not locked in by birth. In real life, many merchants grew very rich. Some married their children into scholar families or bought land. The ranking still mattered, because it told people what kind of life earned honor.

words.d: a set of ideas from the teacher Confucius about respect, duty, learning and good government
a highly educated person; in imperial China, one who studied the classics and could serve in government
a person who earns a living by buying and selling goods

look.title: A Ladder of Honor
look.text: Four people stand on a ladder. On the top rung is a scholar with a book. Below him is a farmer with a hoe. Below the farmer is a potter at his wheel. On the bottom rung is a merchant holding a bag of silver, the heaviest bag on the ladder.
look.prompt: Why might Confucian thinkers place the farmer above the merchant, even though the merchant has more money?

check.q: Which group was at the top of the Confucian ideal order?
check.why: Scholars, educated men who served in government, were placed at the top.

check.q: Why did many Confucian writers rank merchants low?
choices: They saw merchants as not producing things themselves
check.why: Writers said merchants only bought and sold, rather than growing or making things.

check.q: How was China's four-part ranking different from a caste system?
choices: People were not locked in by birth
check.why: The ranking was an ideal of honor; people could move, marry and buy land across it.

lessons.title: The Great Examinations
lessons.mainIdea: China chose many officials through hard written exams, a path upward that lasted until 1905.
reading: Imagine a young man in a small, bare cell, one of thousands in a long row. He has brought food, ink, brushes and a blanket. For days he will write essays on ancient books he has memorized since boyhood. Guards patrol outside. If he passes, his whole family's life may change.

This was the *civil-service examination*. A civil service is the group of officials who run a government. China began using written exams to choose officials about 1,400 years ago. The system grew much larger under the Song dynasty, about a thousand years ago. Tests covered the Confucian classics, poetry and questions of government.

The exams came in levels, from local to provincial to a final exam in the capital. The top degree was called *jinshi*. Only a tiny share of candidates passed the highest levels. The system lasted until the Qing government ended it in 1905, as China sought modern schools.

words.d: a written test used in imperial China to choose government officials
the highest degree in China's examination system
a family that rules a country for many generations

look.title: The Exam System Over Time
look.cite: Benjamin A. Elman, A Cultural History of Civil Examinations in Late Imperial China, 2000
look.prompt: About how many years did China use civil-service exams in some form?

check.q: What is a civil service?
choices: The group of officials who run a government
check.why: A civil service is the body of officials who run a government.

check.q: What did the exams mostly test?
choices: The Confucian classics, poetry and government
check.why: Candidates wrote essays on the Confucian classics, poetry and government questions.

check.q: When did the Qing government end the exams?
check.why: The exams ended in 1905 as China moved toward modern schools.

lessons.title: A Ladder That Was Hard to Climb
lessons.mainIdea: The exams opened a path up in theory, but wealth made it much easier to climb.
reading: In principle, most men could sit for the exams, whatever their family's rank. A farmer's son who studied hard might become a high official. Stories of such success were told and retold. Supporters of the system praised it as a way to reward talent instead of noble birth.

In practice, preparing took many years of study. A family needed money to hire tutors and to spare a son from farm work. So most successful candidates came from families that already had land or learning. Some villages and family groups pooled money to support one bright boy, hoping his success would lift them all.

The exams also shaped who held power in local life. Men who passed even the lower levels joined the *gentry*, a respected class of educated landowners. Women could not take the exams at all. Historians still debate how much the system truly allowed *social mobility*, meaning movement up or down in rank.

words.d: in imperial China, a respected local class of educated landowners, many with exam degrees
the ability of people to move up or down in wealth or rank
a natural ability or skill that can be developed

look.title: Two Boys, One Exam
look.text: Boy A's father owns land and a library. A tutor teaches him every day from age six. Boy B's father rents a small field. Boy B studies at night by a weak lamp after helping in the field. Both are equally bright. Both take the same exam at age twenty.
look.prompt: The exam is the same for both. Is the contest fair? Give one reason for yes and one for no.

check.q: Why did most successful candidates come from wealthy families?
choices: Preparing took years and cost money for tutors
The tests were in a foreign language
check.why: Years of study and tutors cost money that poorer families rarely had.

check.q: What does social mobility mean?
choices: Moving up or down in wealth or rank
check.why: Social mobility is movement up or down in wealth or rank.

check.q: Who could not take China's civil-service exams?
check.why: Women were not allowed to sit for the exams.

lessons.title: Peace and Order After War
lessons.mainIdea: The Tokugawa shoguns ended a long age of war and ruled Japan from about 1603 to 1868.
reading: For more than a hundred years before 1600, Japan was torn by wars between local lords. Then three strong leaders united the country. The last of them, Tokugawa Ieyasu, won a great battle at Sekigahara in 1600. In 1603 he took the title *shogun*, the top military ruler.

Japan still had an emperor in Kyoto, honored as the country's ancient ruler. But the shogun held real power from his city of Edo. The Tokugawa family kept that power for about 265 years. This time is called the Tokugawa or Edo period. It was a long age of peace inside Japan.

The shoguns kept peace partly through strict order. Regional lords, called *daimyo*, had to spend every other year in Edo. Their families stayed there as a guarantee. This rule, called alternate attendance, kept lords loyal and busy. It also cost them great sums on travel.

words.d: the top military ruler of Japan, who held real power while the emperor reigned in name
a regional lord in Japan who ruled land and commanded samurai
the Tokugawa rule that lords live in Edo every other year

look.title: A Lord on the Road
look.text: A long procession winds along a highway. Hundreds of samurai, porters and servants carry chests, banners and a covered chair for their lord. They are traveling to Edo, a trip of many days. The lord must pay for every inn, every meal and every horse.
look.prompt: How might this costly trip, made again and again, help the shogun keep control over the lords?

check.q: Who became shogun in 1603?
check.why: Tokugawa Ieyasu took the title shogun in 1603.

check.q: What was a daimyo?
check.why: Daimyo were regional lords who ruled land and commanded samurai.

check.q: What did the alternate-attendance rule require?
choices: Lords to live in Edo every other year
The emperor to move to Edo
check.why: Lords had to spend every other year in Edo, which kept them loyal and busy.

lessons.title: Samurai, Farmers, Artisans, Merchants
lessons.mainIdea: Tokugawa Japan used a four-rank order with samurai on top and merchants at the bottom.
reading: The Tokugawa borrowed the old Chinese list of four kinds of people. But in Japan, the top rank was not scholars. It was the *samurai*, the warrior class. Samurai made up a small share of the people, often estimated at about 6 percent. Below them came farmers, then artisans, then merchants.

In the long peace, few samurai ever fought a battle. Many worked as officials, clerks and teachers for their lords. They were paid a yearly *stipend* in rice. They had special rights, such as wearing two swords and having family names. A person was born into samurai rank and usually could not leave it.

Below the four ranks were outcast groups, whose jobs, such as leather work, were seen as unclean. They faced harsh separation. Their descendants, known as Burakumin, later organized to fight discrimination, starting in the 1920s. The four-rank order was never a full picture of Japanese life, but it set the rules.

words.d: the hereditary warrior class of Japan, ranked at the top of the Tokugawa order
a fixed regular payment; samurai stipends were paid in rice
passed down from parents to children

look.title: Same List, Different Top
look.text: China's ideal order: scholars, farmers, artisans, merchants. Tokugawa Japan's order: samurai, farmers, artisans, merchants. In China, a man could reach the top by passing exams. In Japan, a man reached the top by being born into a samurai family.
look.prompt: What does the change at the top of the list tell you about what each society honored most?

check.q: Which group was at the top of the Tokugawa order?
check.why: In Japan the samurai, the warrior class, stood at the top.

check.q: How were most samurai paid during the Tokugawa peace?
check.why: Samurai received a yearly stipend paid in rice.

check.q: How did a person usually become a samurai?
choices: By being born into a samurai family
check.why: Samurai rank was hereditary, passed from parents to children.

lessons.title: When Money Outgrew Rank
lessons.mainIdea: Merchants grew rich in Tokugawa cities while many samurai fell into debt.
reading: Peace brought roads, markets and cities. Edo grew into one of the largest cities in the world, with many hundreds of thousands of people. Scholars' estimates for the 1700s run from about 700,000 to a million. Osaka became a great center of rice trading. Merchants handled that rice, lent money and ran large shops. The Mitsui family opened a famous cloth store in Edo in 1673.

Samurai stipends were fixed in rice, but prices and costs kept changing. Many samurai families borrowed from merchants to keep up with their duties. Lords borrowed too. A merchant could hold more wealth than a samurai while still ranking below him.

The government tried *sumptuary laws*, rules limiting what each rank could wear or spend. Merchants were told not to wear silk in public, for example. Many found quiet ways around these rules. City culture, with kabuki theater and colorful woodblock prints, grew from merchant money and tastes.

words.d: rules that limit what people of each rank may wear, own or spend
money that a person owes to someone else

look.title: Great Cities Around 1800
look.cite: Tertius Chandler, Four Thousand Years of Urban Growth, 1987
look.prompt: Edo was among the world's largest cities. Why would a big city give merchants more chances than a village?

check.q: Why did many samurai fall into debt?
choices: Their stipends were fixed while costs changed
They were not allowed to eat rice
Merchants refused to trade with them
They paid high taxes to farmers
check.why: Fixed rice stipends could not keep up with changing prices and costs.

check.q: What were sumptuary laws?
choices: Rules limiting what each rank could wear or spend
check.why: Sumptuary laws set limits on dress and spending by rank.

check.q: Which art forms grew from merchant money and tastes?
check.why: Kabuki and colorful woodblock prints grew from city merchant culture.

lessons.title: A New Government in 1868
lessons.mainIdea: In 1868 reformers restored the emperor's rule and began to rebuild Japan quickly.
reading: In 1853 American warships under Commodore Matthew Perry sailed into Edo Bay. They demanded that Japan open its ports to trade. The shogun's government gave in. Many Japanese feared their country would be taken over by Western powers, as parts of China had been.

Young samurai from southwestern domains, such as Satsuma and Choshu, turned against the shogun. In 1868 they took power in the name of the young Emperor Meiji. This event is called the *Meiji Restoration*. Restoration means bringing back; they said they were bringing back the emperor's rule.

The new leaders moved fast to *modernize*, to build railways, factories, schools and a modern army and navy. They sent students abroad to learn Western science and law. The capital moved to Edo, renamed Tokyo, meaning eastern capital.

words.d: the 1868 change that ended the shogun's rule and put the emperor at the center of a new government
to change a country with new technology, schools and ways of governing

look.title: The Charter Oath
look.text: The new government promised that decisions would be made after wide discussion, that all classes would work together, that common people could follow their own callings, and that knowledge would be sought throughout the world.
look.cite: The Charter Oath, issued in the name of Emperor Meiji, 1868
look.prompt: Which promise in the oath would matter most to a merchant or a farmer? Why?

check.q: What happened in 1853 that alarmed many Japanese?
choices: American warships under Perry demanded open ports
check.why: Perry's warships arrived in 1853 and demanded that Japan open to trade.

check.q: What does restoration mean in Meiji Restoration?
check.why: Restoration means bringing back; leaders said they were restoring the emperor's rule.

check.q: What new name was given to Edo?
check.why: Edo was renamed Tokyo, meaning eastern capital.

lessons.title: The End of the Samurai Class
lessons.mainIdea: Meiji reforms abolished samurai privileges and made all men equal subjects under one law.
reading: The Meiji leaders were mostly samurai themselves. Yet they decided their own class had to go. In 1871 they abolished the lords' domains and made them prefectures run by Tokyo. They declared the four ranks legally equal and ended the separate status of outcast groups, at least on paper.

In 1873 a new law called for *conscription*, drafting young men of every class into a national army. Farmers' sons now carried rifles, a job once reserved for samurai. In 1876 samurai lost their stipends, turned into government bonds, and were banned from wearing swords in public.

Some samurai rebelled. In 1877 Saigo Takamori led the Satsuma Rebellion, the last great samurai uprising. The new army of commoners defeated it. Former samurai found new work as officers, teachers, officials and business owners. Some fell into poverty. A new ranking of nobles and commoners replaced the old one.

words.d: a law that requires people to serve in the military
a special right held only by some people
an armed fight against a government

look.title: Steps in the Meiji Reforms
rows: Domains abolished; four ranks declared equal
look.cite: Marius B. Jansen, The Making of Modern Japan, 2000
look.prompt: How many years passed between the Restoration and the last great samurai rebellion?

check.q: What did conscription change?
choices: Men of every class were drafted into the army
check.why: Conscription drafted young men of every class into a national army.

check.q: What happened in 1876?
choices: Samurai stipends ended and swords were banned in public
check.why: In 1876 stipends were turned into bonds and wearing swords in public was banned.

check.q: Who led the Satsuma Rebellion in 1877?
check.why: Saigo Takamori led the last great samurai uprising.

lessons.title: Korea's Yangban
lessons.mainIdea: In Joseon Korea, the yangban elite gained office through exams, while other classes stood below them.
reading: The Joseon dynasty ruled Korea from 1392 until the early 1900s. Like China, Joseon honored Confucian learning and chose officials through exams called *gwageo*. The families who held office and land were called *yangban*. The name means two groups, for the civil and military officials who stood on two sides of the king.

Below the yangban were several groups. Chungin were skilled specialists, such as interpreters and doctors. Most people were commoners who farmed. At the bottom were the *cheonmin*, the lowborn, including many enslaved people and some workers in low-ranked jobs. Birth mattered a great deal in Joseon.

Joseon also shows that rank could be questioned from the top. King Sejong's scholars created Hangul, a simple Korean alphabet, in the 1440s so that ordinary people could read. In 1894 the Gabo Reforms officially ended class distinctions and slavery in Korea.

words.d: the educated, land-holding elite of Joseon Korea, from whom most officials came
Korea's civil-service examinations
the lowborn class of Joseon Korea, including many enslaved people

look.title: Letters for Everyone
look.text: The king writes that ordinary people often have things they wish to say but cannot write them down. Feeling sorry for them, he has made a small set of new letters, easy to learn and use every day.
look.cite: King Sejong, preface to Hunminjeongeum (The Correct Sounds for Teaching the People), 1446
look.prompt: How might an easy alphabet change the power of the yangban, who could read difficult Chinese characters?

check.q: Who were the yangban?
check.why: The yangban were the elite families who held land and office in Joseon Korea.

check.q: What was the gwageo?
check.why: Gwageo were the exams Joseon used to choose officials.

check.q: What did the Gabo Reforms of 1894 do?
choices: Officially ended class distinctions and slavery
check.why: The Gabo Reforms ended class distinctions and slavery in law.

lessons.title: How Rank Shaped Daily Life
lessons.mainIdea: Rank showed in clothing, speech, homes and manners across East Asia.
reading: In a Joseon town, you could often tell a yangban man at a glance. He might wear a tall black hat made of horsehair and a flowing white robe. He would not carry heavy loads himself. In Tokugawa Japan, a samurai's two swords and hairstyle showed his rank. Clothing was a public badge.

Speech showed rank too. Korean and Japanese both have *honorifics*, special word forms that show respect to someone of higher rank or age. A commoner spoke to a yangban or samurai with humble words. People bowed lower to those above them. These habits of respect remain part of both languages today, though now they mostly follow age and role.

Rank shaped homes, marriages and even where people could live. Yet people pushed back. Merchants bought fine goods quietly. Farmers sometimes protested unfair taxes in large groups. Rank was powerful, but people were never simply their rank.

words.d: special word forms that show respect to someone of higher rank or age
a person's position or rank in a society

look.title: A Street in Seoul, About 1800
look.text: A man in a tall black horsehair hat and white robe walks slowly. A servant walks behind him carrying his books. A farmer with a heavy bundle on a wooden A-frame steps aside and lowers his head. A doctor from the chungin class nods politely to both.
look.prompt: List three clues in this scene that show each person's rank.

check.q: What are honorifics?
check.why: Honorifics are special word forms that show respect to someone of higher rank or age.

check.q: Which item showed a samurai's rank in public?
check.why: Samurai wore two swords as a public sign of their rank.

check.q: Which statement best fits the lesson?
choices: Rank had no effect on daily life
Rank was powerful, but people found ways to push back
check.why: Merchants and farmers pushed back in quiet and open ways even under strict rank rules.

review.q: In China's ideal order, which group was ranked lowest?
review.why: Confucian writers placed merchants last because they did not produce goods.

review.q: How did China's top rank differ from Japan's?
choices: China's top was scholars chosen by exams; Japan's was samurai by birth
China's top was samurai; Japan's was scholars
review.why: China honored exam-trained scholars; Tokugawa Japan honored hereditary samurai.

review.q: Which fact shows the exams did not give everyone an equal chance?
choices: Wealthy families could pay for years of tutoring
The exams were held in cells
review.why: Preparation cost money, so wealthy families had a big advantage.

review.q: What best describes the puzzle of merchants in Tokugawa Japan?
choices: They could not live in cities
They were often rich but ranked lowest
review.why: Merchants often held great wealth while ranking at the bottom of the official order.

review.q: What did the Meiji conscription law of 1873 show?
choices: Commoners could now serve as soldiers
review.why: Conscription drafted men of every class, ending the samurai monopoly on fighting.

review.q: Which group in Joseon Korea included interpreters and doctors?
review.why: Chungin were skilled specialists such as interpreters and doctors.

review.q: What do the Gabo Reforms of 1894 and the Meiji reforms of 1871 have in common?
choices: Both officially ended old class ranks
review.why: Both reforms declared an end to old legal class distinctions.
